1:
Gill notes that Hannah had prayed before, but silently, and this is vocal; she had been answered, and now gives thanks, thanksgiving being itself a kind of prayer, which is why the narrative calls a song a prayer. Wesley agrees. Henry makes most of it: in every address to God we must express a grateful regard to him as our benefactor; what we win by prayer we may wear with comfort, and must wear with praise, and thanks for mercies received shall be accepted as a petition for further mercy. She does not commend Samuel for the prettiest child or the most toward for his age, as fond parents are apt to do, but overlooks the gift and praises the giver. There may be other Samuels, he says, but no other Jehovah. Four attributes are celebrated in the opening lines on his reckoning: unspotted purity, almighty power, unsearchable wisdom and unerring justice, by which last men's actions are weighed. The song stands on record, he adds, to encourage those of the weaker sex to attend the throne of grace.

That the song is prophecy is urged on several grounds. Gill cites the Targum for a spirit of prophecy and reports that the Jews reckon Hannah one of the seven prophetesses, finding here not only her experience of divine goodness but things to be done hereafter in Israel, and particularly the Messiah. Clarke calls it an oracular declaration rather than a prayer, every part having respect to the future. He quotes Hales, who finds it excelling in simplicity and uniformity of sentiment, exalting the humble-minded and abasing the arrogant, and ranks Hannah a prophetess of the first class for describing the promised Saviour as a King before there was any king in Israel, and for first applying the epithet which is Messiah in Hebrew, Christ in Greek and Anointed in English. Kimchi, he adds, was so struck by the language that he ingenuously confessed the King of whom Hannah speaks is the Messiah, a tradition founded chiefly on Balaam having taught Israel that a great king should arise. He notes that the best manuscripts write the hymn in poetic lines, and prints it so, judging from the connection that she delivered it at her son's dedication rather than, as some think, at his birth.

Keil and Ellicott reach the same height by another road, and in nearly the same words. Keil calls the psalm the mature fruit of the Spirit of God, and says the pious woman discerned in her own experience the general laws of the divine economy; what she had known of his gracious government while bowed down was a pledge that the nation, then deeply oppressed, would likewise be lifted up. Ellicott makes the movement personal first. She had been an unhappy woman, her life as she thought a failure and her dearest hopes baffled, and had fled to the Rock of Israel and found rest, and then joy; the hymn afterwards became one of the loved songs of the people, handed down in the words that first fell from her. He also cautions against a misreading of her boast: mine horn is exalted does not mean I am proud but I am strong, mighty now in the gift received; the image comes from oxen, and grew familiar to a shepherd-people. Clarke agrees that horn means power and dominion and finds the sentiment among the heathen too, quoting Horace, who tells his wine-jar that it adds strength and horns to the poor man. Henry hears music rather than cattle, David's singers having been appointed to lift up the horn, so that the phrase means her praises are elevated to an unusual strain. On the enlarged mouth he and Wesley agree that she now has wherewith to answer those who reproached her, Wesley adding that she shows her modesty by not naming Peninnah, only her enemies in general.
2:
On the holiness Gill piles up adverbs: God is essentially, originally, independently, perfectly and immutably holy, as others are not. Angels are holy, but not of themselves, and cover their faces while celebrating that perfection; nor is theirs naturally unchangeable, as the fall of some demonstrates. Among men some were holy only in a typical sense, some outwardly before others but not before God, and even in the truly sanctified there is a likeness only. Wesley puts it briefly: none is holy besides God, save by participation. Clarke turns the claim outward: holiness is peculiar to the God of Israel, and no false god ever pretended to it, nor any religion professed before the true revelation. Keil explains why the reason given is that there is none beside him: holiness is simply the moral reflection of the glory of the one absolute God, so that the wicked should tremble before it rather than boast of lofty things.

The rock draws two different derivations. Clarke reports Rabbi Maimon's observation that the word, applied to Jehovah, means fountain or spring, and concludes that no source of continual help exists but our God. Ellicott keeps the stone and traces the image to the desert wandering, where the strange fantastic crags of Sinai, standing up amid shifting sands, supplied a picture of unchangeableness and security. The term is first found in the Song of Moses, where the juxtaposition of rock and salvation suggests Hannah knew that national hymn, and names like Zurishaddai and Zuriel prove the usage current already in his day. Wesley reduces the figure to comfort: thou only art a refuge to all that flee to thee.

Whom the warning against proud talk addresses is agreed. Gill takes it of Peninnah and her allies, whose mouths would now be stopped; Wesley adds that she speaks in the plural so as not to expose her rival's name, and hears in the God of knowledge a rebuke aimed at what Peninnah's conscience knew. On the closing verb the two who study it disagree. Clarke renders it that actions are directed, and draws from that how by his counsel alone can we begin, continue or end any work. Ellicott keeps weighed, notes the Hebrew order putting a God of knowledge first, and quotes Rabbi Ami in the Talmud, that knowledge is of great price because it stands between two divine names. He adds that this is one of fifteen places where the Masorites read a negative particle instead as the word meaning by him.

From the attributes Hannah turns to the reversals. Gill takes bows for all military arms, which God can break so as to make war cease, and adds that Satan's are broken likewise and his fiery darts quenched. Ellicott quotes Von Gerlach for the principle: every power that will be something in itself is destroyed by the Lord, and every weakness that despairs of itself is transformed into power. The heroes of the bow, he notes, are named by their weapon, poetically put first instead of its bearer. Clarke reports the Targum's reading of the reversals as a series of prophecies, against the Philistines, Sennacherib, Nebuchadnezzar, the Greeks and Haman; but for himself he thinks these things frequently happen in the ordinary course, and that it is the particular providence of God which Hannah celebrates through this simple yet sublime ode. Keil glosses the barren bearing seven, that being the full number of the divine blessing, while the mother of many pines away, having lost her sons and with them her support in old age. Ellicott says the thought reverts here to Hannah, and reports a curious legend that for each boy born to her two of Peninnah's died; Wesley takes seven for many and hears the prophetic style, the past put for the future, Hannah counting on more children from some assurance given her or from Eli's prediction.
6:
On killing and making alive Gill reads a double sense: God removes some by death and preserves others, and of one man can do both, Kimchi and Ben Gersom referring the second clause to the resurrection; spiritually he kills by the law and quickens by his Spirit. Wesley keeps it personal, she who was almost consumed with grief having been revived, and notes that death often names a calamity. Clarke examines the word rendered grave. It covers the tomb, the state of the dead and the invisible place of spirits; we sometimes render it hell, but since that comes from the Saxon for to conceal it means only the covered place. The Targum, he adds, reads a resurrection here, God sending men down so that in time to come he may bring them into the lives of eternity. Ellicott insists that nothing in human affairs is the sport of blind chance, and reports a Talmudic tradition that Hannah's words describe an intermediate class at the judgment, sealed at once neither for life nor for hell, who go down and cry awhile and then ascend.

Gill takes poverty and wealth alike for gifts of providence, the difference between men being contrived so that they depend on one another. Clarke turns it into a question of trust: many cannot bear affluence, and if God kept entrusting them with it their ruin would follow, while some he trusts and makes stewards of his secular bounty. On the beggar lifted from the dunghill Gill again doubles the sense: the literal poor sitting in the dust, and the poor in spirit who alone are beggars, since those who do not feel their want never ask. Clarke prefers instances, and names three raised from a dungeon to a throne: Cincinnatus, Joseph, and Roushen Akhter, exalted over Hindustan, on whom an elegant couplet was made playing on his name, which means a bright star — he was a bright star, but now is become a moon; Joseph is taken from prison, and is a king. Wesley notes that the exalted inherit their throne and transmit it to their posterity, and that he who set the pillars under the earth may dispose of the persons on it as he pleases. Ellicott finds the cosmogony fitted to the childhood of peoples, and adds a rueful question: whether after three or four thousand years, with modern science round us, we know much more of how the universe is made and governed. Jerome rendered the word hinges and Gesenius foundations, but he thinks pillars best.

With the keeping of the saints' feet Gill says the promises begin. Ellicott calls it the comforting deduction Hannah drew from her own life, set down for the solace of true servants after her: since Jehovah governs the world, only the wicked have reason to be afraid. He matches the closing line with the prophet's not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, and with the word given to Paul, that strength is perfected in weakness. Wesley glosses the silence of the wicked as a stopping of mouths that once opened wide against heaven. On the last verse Gill and Clarke take the contenders for real enemies, Ben Gersom applying the prophecy to the Philistines whom Samuel discomfited, while Clarke extends the judging of the earth to the preaching of the Gospel and cites the Targum for multiplying Messiah's reign. Ellicott makes the strongest claim: this is the first passage in the Old Testament to name his Anointed, Jewish expositors have generally read it of King Messiah, and A Lapide said all these things have regard to Christ, David's reign and Solomon's being a pale reflection of the glory expected. Keil, whose note runs into the next scene, observes that Elkanah then went back to Ramah, the silence about his wives being no warrant for Thenius to send him home alone.
11:
Henry sets out the design of the passage: two households are interwoven throughout, as if the historian meant to set one against the other, the devotion of Elkanah's family aggravating the iniquity of Eli's, and the sons' wickedness making Samuel's piety shine brighter. Eli's house sat at the tabernacle door, and Henry draws the moral that the nearer the church the further from God. Nothing appears against Eli himself, who no doubt taught his sons well and prayed for them, yet they grew up profane, which proves that parents cannot give grace to their children nor does it run in the blood; their birth only aggravated the offence, since they lived at the fountain-head of ministry. Of the boy's service Henry is charmingly concrete: Samuel could light a candle, hold a dish, run an errand or shut a door, and because he did it with a pious mind it is called ministering to the Lord. Wesley suggests singing or lighting the lamps as work fit for such years, and reads before Eli as under his inspection. Ellicott has him living under the shadow of the sanctuary, ministering with his child powers before the altar of the Invisible and trained by the old high priest.

On the name Belial Ellicott corrects a common impression: the English prints it as though it were a pagan deity, but it merely signifies worthlessness, and the capital probably comes from Paul's contrast between Christ and Belial. Keil glosses the second clause to mean they did not know the Lord as he should be known, that is, did not fear him. Clarke calls them devil's children, and makes an axiom of it: an impious priesthood is the grand cause of a nation's ruin. Ellicott quotes Dean Stanley to the same effect: the three-pronged fork that fishes up the seething flesh is the earliest type of scrambling after preferment by base means, and the profligacy at the tabernacle door the type of many a later scandal.

Gill stresses that the custom was no law of God but a practice the sons introduced, which the other priests followed until it had statutory force; Keil says the word rendered custom means a right they had usurped, and follows the servant thrusting his fork into the pot and the priest taking whatever it raised. Clarke sets the lawful shares against it — breast and shoulder to the priest, the fat on the altar, the rest to the offerer — and observes that under pretence of taking their own they took the best and as much as they chose; Wesley adds that they snatched even that before it was waved. The demand for raw flesh all treat as the graver crime. Clarke says they would serve themselves before God was served, the priest preferring roast to boiled and lifting it from the pot if he found it there. Ellicott calls it a contemptuous insult, the fat being God's portion, so that seizing the flesh first amounted to robbing God. Henry notices to Israel's honour that the people, tamely yielding their own rights, were still anxious that God should not be robbed, and begged that the fat be burnt first; it was a shame that priests needed admonishing by the laity.

On the effect the voices divide. Keil quotes Von Gerlach that the robbery was a small sin beside the contempt of the sacrifices they spread among the people, and Ellicott cites A Lapide on the stumbling-block laid before the laity. Clarke traces the line further: seeing the priests had no piety and acted as though there were no God, the people despised his service. Wesley alone will not let the people off. The efficacy of the sacraments does not depend on the goodness of those who administer them, so it was folly and sin in them to think the worse of God's institutions, though the greater sin lay with the priests.
18:
Gill explains why the boy's ministry is mentioned both before and after the account of Eli's sons: partly to their shame, partly to Samuel's honour, that he was not corrupted by their practices. He also marks a change of phrase. Earlier the child ministered before Eli, under his direction; here before the Lord, in higher services needing no such help. Gill takes this to belong to a later stage of growth, though related here, and notes that he is still called a child. Ellicott finds a deliberate contrast between the covetous ministrations of the worldly priests and the quiet service of the boy his parents had devoted to the sanctuary. Wesley reads the verb as discharging his office faithfully, and the place as the tabernacle.

The linen ephod is described by all, with one dissent about who might wear it. Keil calls it a shoulder-dress resembling the high priest's in shape but made of plain white cloth; all the priests wore such then, and David wore one at a religious festival. Samuel received it as a boy, being set apart to a lifelong service. Ellicott describes the make, two pieces resting on the shoulders before and behind, joined at the top and fastened with a girdle, and calls it an official garment given with the high priest's sanction. Wesley alone raises the difficulty of the wearer: the dress was allowed not only to inferior priests and Levites but to eminent persons among the people, and so to Samuel, no Levite but a Nazarite. Clarke leaves the garment for the word, reporting that the Targum renders it a cardit of byssus, a term apparently borrowed from the Greek for a sleeved tunic the Romans thought effeminate.

The little coat draws out the domestic detail. Gill notes that the word is that used for the priest's robe, and that Hannah very likely spun, wove and made it herself, partly from love and partly to lessen the charge of keeping him; the Talmudists allow a priest to minister in a garment his mother made. Keil takes it for a smaller version of the high priest's robe, of simpler stuff and without the symbolical ornaments on the hem. Clarke is more practical, calling it a cloak or surtout to keep the boy from the cold and save his other clothes from being spoiled in his meaner services, and supposes a new one each year. Ellicott looks past the cloth to the intention, taking the dress to have been arranged by Eli, who saw the child destined for some great work and, aware what his own sons were, hoped to train this favoured boy as his successor in the chief office in Israel.

Gill says Eli pronounced the blessing not only the first time but every year they came up. Keil paraphrases the wish as asking that the Lord lend Elkanah seed of this woman in place of the one asked for, and explains the odd third person as indefinite: though Hannah prayed in Eli's sight, he might fairly assume the father shared her desire. Clarke alone thinks the passage disordered. The natural place of this verse seems to him before the eleventh, with the twenty-first following and perhaps the twenty-sixth after, the subjects of the chapter being much entangled by the wrong position of the verses. Keil takes the opposite view of the same seam, insisting the particle joining the blessing to its fulfilment is neither a conditional nor a copyist's error; one need only supply the thought that Eli's word was no empty wish, and read that they went home blessed, for the Lord visited Hannah. Gill agrees that the visitation confirmed the blessing, and Wesley closes on the boy, who grew not only in age and stature but in wisdom and goodness, and grew so before the Lord, not merely before men, who may be deceived, but under an all-seeing eye.
22:
Eli's age is treated as explanation, and by some as excuse. Gill reckons him about ninety, since he died at ninety-eight, and thinks the note shows his incapacity for office, which gave his sons their chance; it also accounts for the gentleness of the reproof, age having left him less spirit and his sons being grown. Yet Gill will not let that stand as a defence: he ought to have considered himself not a father only but high priest and judge. Wesley reasons the same way. Ellicott hears something warmer in it, holding that the compiler plainly wished to speak as kindly of Eli as he could, dwelling on his piety, his love for Samuel and his patriotism, so that here, where his sons' conduct is at its worst, an excuse is offered for the father: he was very old.

Of the women at the tabernacle door little is claimed and much guessed. Clarke supposes they had some employment there, citing the same phrase in Exodus; Ellicott thinks they may have assisted in the liturgy, comparing the psalm about the great company of female singers, and adds that here, as so often, immorality follows on unbelief. Wesley explains the place: the door was where the people waited when they came up, since the altar stood by it. Keil observes that the crime is learned only from the reproof itself, so that beside robbing the offerings they profaned the sanctuary with whoredom; this whole people means everyone who came to Shiloh and saw.

The rebuke satisfies nobody. Gill says the sins deserved a sharper reprimand and worse than words, Eli being bound as judge to punish. Clarke draws the character: a fondly affectionate, easy father who wished his sons well but never brought them under discipline nor used his authority to restrain them, though as judge he could have cast them out at once; his ruin and theirs followed. Wesley states the fault precisely: the sin was not only that he reproved too gently but that he rested in a rebuke and inflicted none of the punishments such crimes deserved. Gill objects even to the address, my sons being too endearing for men who deserved the name of Belial. Keil notes a play in the Hebrew that cannot be carried over: the verb means to decide a case, then to arbitrate, then in another form to entreat, so that when a man sins against man God settles the dispute through the authorities, but when a man sins against God none can interpose. Ellicott says this touches the mystery of sin, one transgression seeming to lie beyond forgiveness, of which the Redeemer warned as the sin against the Holy Ghost. Clarke turns the question into a gospel answer: the law fixed which sins were capital and allowed no appeal, whereas John writes that if any man sin we have an Advocate with the Father.

On the reason they would not hear, the three who address it differ sharply. Ellicott takes the resolution to slay them as founded on the eternal foreknowledge of their persistence, and thinks a period comes in a sinner's life when the Spirit ceases to plead and he is left to himself. Wesley says they had sinned away their day of grace and hardened their hearts, till God gave them up. Clarke rejects the whole construction as a mistranslation. The particle rendered because should be rendered therefore, as Noldius takes it here: they would not hearken, therefore God purposed to destroy them. It was their not hearkening, he insists, that induced the Lord to will their destruction. Against all this the boy is set once more. Gill notes that Samuel grew better while Eli's sons grew worse, the contrast making one shine and the other look blacker; Ellicott observes that Luke afterwards borrowed the biographer's words to describe the boyhood of one far greater than the child-prophet of Israel.
27:
Who the man of God was nobody can say, and the guessing is itself instructive. Gill canvasses the candidates: Ben Gersom and Abarbinel propose Phinehas, impossible, since had he lived Eli would not have been high priest; the older Jews and Jarchi name Elkanah, whom the Targum makes a disciple of the prophets, though Scripture never calls him one; others suggest Samuel, concealing his name from modesty, but he was still a child. Ellicott declines the whole business. This messenger appears suddenly at Shiloh, nameless and homeless, delivers his doom, and disappears; the title occurs some forty times in Judges, Samuel and Kings, and no prophet had been named in Israel's story since Deborah. Henry explains why the message came, and why to the father rather than the sons: Eli had reproved too gently, so God sent a prophet to reprove him sharply, and sent it to Eli because he meant to save him, having already determined to destroy his sons. If good men fail in their duty and by their remissness contribute to the sin of sinners, they must expect both to hear of it and to smart for it.

The opening questions are not questions. Ellicott says they ask nothing but appeal to Eli's conscience, the old man answering each with a silent yes. Clarke and Ellicott agree that the house of thy father means Aaron, from whom through Ithamar Eli was descended; Clarke traces the office from Aaron to Eleazar and Phinehas, then into the younger branch, and back again because of the profligacy of Eli's sons. Keil sets out the three clauses defining the priesthood: to ascend the altar, that is, to perform the sacrificial worship; to kindle incense, standing for the holy place; and to wear the ephod, for the holy of holies. Ellicott adds that the ephod carried the Urim and Thummim, by which the invisible King's will was sought. Henry sums the recital as an aggravation: what more could God have done to engage them, and such favours will be remembered against us if we profane our crown.

On the charge of kicking Gill hears a metaphor from cattle well fed and fat, which spurn even those who feed them, and reports the Targum's harder reading, that they took the holy offerings by force. Ellicott traces the image to the song of Moses, where Jeshurun waxed fat and kicked, a pampered beast growing unmanageable and refusing obedience to a kind master. Keil observes that the reproof falls first on the priests generally, Eli included, since he had not resisted the abuses, and narrows to him only in the words about honouring his sons. Clarke and Wesley read that clause as connivance, Eli choosing rather to offend God by his silence than to displease his sons. Ellicott suspects a second motive besides foolish fondness: unwillingness to divert from his family the rich revenue flowing from the pilgrims' offerings, which is why he kept these covetous men as his representatives and let things drift.

The revocation raises a question about the promise. Clarke holds the pledge of a perpetual priesthood, though it looks absolute, to be conditional like all such promises, the condition implied though not expressed, so that unworthy walking annuls it; Ellicott says the same, a covenant of walking depending on those who walk, and Wesley states flatly that God retracts what he promised. Keil disputes something narrower: C. a Lapide takes the earlier saying to mean the high priesthood was transferred from Eleazar's family to Ithamar's and promised to Eli's descendants for all time, which Keil holds at variance with the facts, the promise running to the whole priesthood rather than Eli's line. What none of them qualifies is the rule that follows. Clarke calls it a plan from which God never departs, underlying every promise: them that honour me I will honour, and they that despise me shall be lightly esteemed.
31:
All read the cutting off of the arm as the destruction of strength. Keil explains that a family's strength lies in the vital energy of its members, showing itself in their reaching a good old age instead of pining away early; that would now fail. Ellicott adds that sickness or the sword would consume its members young, the sentence being repeated twice more in different words. Wesley canvasses what the arm was: the ark, called God's strength in the psalm and Eli's too, since he could not bear the news of its loss; or his priestly dignity; or, likeliest, his children. Gill notes that the threat took effect quickly, in the days of Eli's sons, and was complete in eighty years.

The enemy in the habitation divides them, and Clarke observes that almost every version and commentator takes the clause differently. He reads the word as calamity rather than rival, finding it in the defeat of Israel, the capture of the ark and the death of his sons, all known to Eli before his own tragical end. Wesley reads it the same way, of the affliction of the sanctuary, whose chief glory was the ark and chief disaster its loss. Gill prefers the rival reading, of Solomon's time, when Abiathar of Eli's family was thrust out and Zadok put in. Ellicott weighs both and prefers the ark: the earthly habitation of the Eternal was robbed of its glory, the ark being the heart of the sanctuary. Keil takes a third course: in all the benefits conferred on his people Eli would see only distress for the dwelling, the tabernacle falling further into decay; and since the high priest is addressed as custodian, the words bind his whole house.

The next threat is a refinement of cruelty. Keil pairs its clauses with the thoughts before: someone of Eli's family would always serve at the altar, precisely so that he might watch the decay and pine away. Ellicott points to the last verse for the sense: those not cut off in youth would be worse off than those who were, since they must beg their bread. Wesley puts the flower of their age at about thirty, when they would have entered on their office. Of the sign all agree, Clarke and Ellicott pointing to the battle where both sons fell and the ark was taken, Keil noting that Eli saw it but did not long survive.

Who the faithful priest is remains the sharpest question in the chapter. Gill names Zadok, put into the office by Solomon in Abiathar's room, and rejects Samuel, who was not of the priestly race and had no sure house, his sons having declined from the ways of truth. Clarke and Wesley agree on Zadok, Wesley adding that this confirmed the everlasting priesthood covenanted to Phinehas of Eleazar's line and broken awhile by Eli of Ithamar's. Ellicott argues at length for Samuel, who succeeded Eli in most of his functions, ministered as a priest though no son of Aaron, and stood as mediator in sacrifice and intercession, walking before the anointed Saul; the sure house he finds in his posterity, Heman his grandson being seer to the king. Against Zadok he presses a difficulty he calls insurmountable: whether so obscure a man, generations later and overshadowed by Solomon's splendour, can be what these magnificent promises mean. Keil reports Ephraem Syrus taking both, Samuel succeeding to the government and Zadok to the office. Ellicott also refuses those who find Christ in the faithful priest, since this priest walks before the Lord's Anointed; Wesley finds Christ exactly there, the high priest being a type who went before him as John afterwards did. Keil glosses the coin as a small piece got by begging singly; Clarke turns the picture into a warning, since they who once fed to the full on the Lord's sacrifices now beg a morsel of bread.
